what: Viavi Solutions makes test equipment and optical components. Its instruments check that fibre-optic networks, data centres and mobile networks actually work, and its optical filters sit inside anti-counterfeiting inks, 3D sensing modules and other specialist uses.
customers: Telecom carriers, cable operators, data centre builders, network equipment makers and contractors who install fibre. The optical coatings business sells to currency printers and to consumer electronics makers.
money: Field and lab instruments for installing and troubleshooting fibre and wireless networks.
Pigments used in banknote anti-counterfeiting, plus optical filters for 3D sensing and other uses.
Software and systems carriers use to monitor live networks.
moat: Test instruments become the standard a carrier's technicians are trained on, and the measurement results must be comparable across years, so changing vendor is disruptive. The anti-counterfeiting pigment business is a near-sole-source arrangement with national currency printers.
risks: Earnings are small relative to the price: about $67.0M of net income gives a price/earnings ratio near 113.
Revenue dipped from $1.3B in 2022 to $1.0B in 2024 before recovering to $1.5B, showing how sharply carrier spending cycles swing.
Carrier capital budgets are decided annually and can be cut quickly, and a handful of large customers shape a quarter.
Currency anti-counterfeiting demand depends on how often national banks redesign notes, which is lumpy and unpredictable.
Debt of $684.9M roughly matches the $649.8M cash balance, leaving little net cushion.
opportunities: Data centre build-out needs high-speed optical test equipment, and Viavi sells into exactly that upgrade cycle.
Revenue has turned up strongly, from $1.1B to $1.5B in the most recent year shown.
Operating leverage is high: because much of the cost base is fixed, recovering revenue flows through to profit quickly.
The seven analysts covering it average a $56.00 target, well above the current $29.37 price, though such a wide gap deserves scepticism.
watch: Orders rather than revenue. In test equipment, bookings turn before shipments, so the order book tells you whether the data centre and fibre upgrade cycle is still feeding the business.
